title: Exam Deadline Map
user: A self-directed learner with an exam date who needs a realistic day-by-day revision plan without turning every deck up to maximum intensity for months.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says vocabulary learners do the usual streaks and flashcards for months yet still forget words when they need them.
A learner explicitly requests a deadline-aware 0.95-retention plan that bounds daily cramming time instead of a single year-round retention setting.

recurrence: Two 2026 communities describe the same planning failure: long-term review controls do not translate into a bounded plan for a real date; the consequence is either panic cramming or avoidance.
current_workaround: Raise Anki desired retention by hand, make a spreadsheet, or cram the backlog in the final week.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki/FSRS schedules recall and RemNote offers exam dates, but neither makes a transparent, time-capped what-to-study calendar from an exported deck the primary product.
smallest_useful_product: A local web app importing Anki CSV/review counts, an exam date, and daily minutes to produce a review/new-card calendar with overload warnings. Non-goals: replacing Anki, inventing card content, or proctoring.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 70% of users with a deadline follow the plan on at least 20 days and no planned day exceeds their stated time cap by more than 15 minutes.
monetization: one-time — deadline planning is episodic and users should retain their study data locally.
constraints: All deck data stays in-browser; forecast assumptions must be shown and editable; explicitly state that it is planning support, not a prediction of exam results.
why_distinct: It is a constrained revision calendar over existing recall history, not another flashcard client or generic to-do list.

title: Time Budget New Cards
user: An Anki or CSV-flashcard learner who needs to choose how many new items to introduce within a fixed daily study budget despite mixed difficulty.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A vocabulary learner reports using ten-minute sessions and another participant rejects rote flashcards in favor of sentence production.
A language learner asks FSRS to vary new-card count with difficulty because 20 easy nouns and 20 abstract grammar cards consume radically different time.

recurrence: Independent 2025 vocabulary and FSRS users optimize for limited time rather than arbitrary card count; a bad new-card setting makes the habit unsustainable.
current_workaround: Set one fixed daily-new-card number, manually lower it after a hard day, or stop adding cards entirely.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki and FSRS expose counts, intervals, and retention; they do not offer a simple time-budget recommendation before the learner starts a session.
smallest_useful_product: An offline companion that ingests review duration/history or a CSV, estimates the marginal time cost of new cards, and recommends today’s safe new-card cap. Non-goals: changing the scheduler or generating cards.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot users remain within ±20% of their chosen study budget for 21 of 30 days while continuing to add new material.
monetization: free — a transparent companion must earn trust; export-friendly usage can build adoption.
constraints: Do not claim clinical learning optimization; estimates must disclose uncertainty and support manual correction; no account is required.
why_distinct: The controlled variable is minutes and cognitive load, rather than another queue that assumes every card costs the same.

title: Importance Weighted Review
user: A learner maintaining a large mixed-value deck who needs common, high-impact concepts to receive more reliable recall than long-tail facts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker identifies retaining domain knowledge alongside technical concepts as a separate, difficult problem that current learning tools overlook.
A Cantonese learner requests different retention targets by a note’s character-frequency field so common characters get more attention.

recurrence: Two 2025 requests center on prioritization rather than merely accumulating cards; the severity rises with large vocational or language decks.
current_workaround: Split decks manually, tag important facts, or set one blunt desired-retention target for everything.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki supports tags and FSRS supports a deck-level target, but neither offers an auditable importance-to-review-policy layer for imported cards.
smallest_useful_product: A local CSV/Anki-export policy editor that maps tags or numeric fields such as frequency, exam weight, and safety criticality to review targets, then previews added workload and exports settings. Non-goals: proprietary corpus ranking or medical advice.
success_measure: In a four-week test, users can identify their top-priority 20% of cards and report at least 90% recall on a sampled priority set without increasing total daily time more than 25%.
monetization: one-time — it is a durable personal-study configuration tool with no need to host content.
constraints: Imported fields can expose sensitive study topics; process locally and preserve original exports; labels must never imply objective importance.
why_distinct: It adds transparent value weighting to an existing scheduler instead of claiming an opaque model knows what a learner should study.

title: Review Backlog Forecast
user: A spaced-repetition learner returning after missed days who needs to recover a backlog without silently losing progress or creating one impossible session.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A flashcard user questions why apps require subjective Good/Average/Bad ratings, surfacing the lack of understandable feedback about what the queue is doing.
The requester wants today’s cards included when rescheduling overdue material because leaving them untouched can still cause progress loss.

recurrence: Both 2025 discussions show learners cannot see or control the consequences of scheduling choices; backlogs turn a routine into a demoralizing unknown.
current_workaround: Click reschedule, bury cards, skip reviews, or work through the pile until fatigue sets in.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki offers rescheduling actions and review counts, while FSRS optimizes intervals; neither provides a plain-language recovery simulation before the learner changes cards.
smallest_useful_product: A local import-and-preview tool that models three recovery policies (steady, deadline, gentle), shows cards/minutes per day and exactly which assumptions move cards. Non-goals: modifying Anki collections or guaranteeing retention.
success_measure: At least 65% of returning pilot users choose a plan and reduce an overdue queue by 50% within 14 days without any planned session exceeding their cap.
monetization: free — recovery transparency is a narrow trust-building utility, not an engagement product.
constraints: Simulation must be reversible and clearly distinguish estimates from actual Anki scheduling; no collection credentials or sync access.
why_distinct: It explains and forecasts a backlog before rescheduling, rather than presenting another set of opaque review buttons.

title: Focus Study Sprint
user: A student or self-learner who wants short, calm, active-recall sessions without streaks, rewards, feeds, or an AI content firehose.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo language-app maker reports deliberately avoiding gamification, streaks, subscriptions, and engagement tricks and asks whether calm learning can work.
The request for card-specific desired retention highlights how much complexity sits behind a supposedly simple review flow.

recurrence: 2025 learners and builders are explicitly resisting engagement mechanics while still needing enough structure to practice; complexity often leaks into the learner’s session.
current_workaround: Use a Pomodoro timer beside Anki/Quizlet, dismiss reward screens, or abandon apps that optimize streaks.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo and Quizlet optimize engagement; Anki optimizes flexible scheduling. There is room for a deliberately finite, local recall session that foregrounds completion over return frequency.
smallest_useful_product: A PWA where users paste 5–30 prompts, choose 5/10/20 minutes, answer in a distraction-free loop, and receive a private session recap with no streak or leaderboard. Non-goals: generated lessons, social feeds, and habit nudges.
success_measure: Among 30 early users, at least half complete three or more voluntary sessions/week while fewer than 10% enable a reminder.
monetization: one-time — calm, local practice should not require a recurring attention tax.
constraints: No behavioral analytics by default; accessibility needs keyboard-first operation, reduced motion, and screen-reader labels; do not make learning claims beyond practice support.
why_distinct: The product constraint is intentional absence of engagement loops and generated content, not a thinner Duolingo clone.

title: Audio Gap Loop
user: A language learner or parent helping a child who needs repeatable listen-say-check practice from short audio without addictive gamification.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent asks for a child-suitable language app that is not heavily addictive or gamified; replies emphasize repeated speaking practice and replaying familiar media.
Anki users debate audio-aware auto-advance timing because a fixed seconds setting should not cut across an audio-led practice flow.

recurrence: In 2025, both a parent and flashcard users point to precise repetition timing as core learning infrastructure, while mainstream language apps are commonly gamified.
current_workaround: Replay clips in a media player, make audio Anki cards, or use Duolingo despite its incentive design.
incumbents_and_gap: Pimsleur and Glossika offer paid audio courses; Anki supports audio cards. Neither is a tiny bring-your-own-audio loop with silence gaps, slowed replay, and no game layer.
smallest_useful_product: A browser-only audio practice player: import personally owned clips, mark a transcript line, set listen/pause/repeat cadence, and keep a local completion log. Non-goals: speech scoring, a licensed media catalog, or child data collection.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot users create ten loops and complete 50 repetitions across three weeks, with median setup under two minutes per clip.
monetization: one-time — personal audio stays on-device and server costs are unnecessary.
constraints: Users must supply material they may use; preserve all audio locally; include hearing-safe volume guidance and accessible transcript controls.
why_distinct: It is a configurable cadence tool for owned audio, not another course, chatbot, or unreliable pronunciation grader.

title: Parallel Reader
user: An intermediate language learner with legitimately obtained EPUBs in two languages who needs synchronized reading, audio, and private word capture.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner explicitly asks whether a tool can align two EPUB editions side by side with synchronized scrolling/highlighting, translation, and audiobook support.

Anki users report that pasted image material becomes base64 data, bloating collections and slowing image-occlusion study—evidence that media-heavy personal study material needs careful local handling.

recurrence: The 2025 request names the missing combined reader directly, while a separate 2025 issue demonstrates the friction of moving rich study material into a flashcard database.
current_workaround: Open two readers, scroll manually, use Readlang/LingQ with their catalog constraints, or paste excerpts and screenshots into cards.
incumbents_and_gap: LingQ and Readlang support assisted reading; Kindle supports books; Anki captures words. The gap is a private BYO dual-EPUB workspace with synchronization and exportable word snippets.
smallest_useful_product: An offline web reader for two DRM-free EPUBs with chapter alignment, manual paragraph anchors, side-by-side mode, and TSV export of selected sentence pairs. Non-goals: selling books, DRM removal, machine translation, or public sharing.
success_measure: At least 50% of test users align one full chapter in under ten minutes and export 20 useful sentence pairs after one week.
monetization: one-time — personal-library tooling has clear local value without hosted content costs.
constraints: Accept only DRM-free files; no included copyrighted text; keep books and selections in IndexedDB/local export; make alignment manual and reversible.
why_distinct: It connects the learner’s own parallel editions and audio workflow without trying to become a licensed-content library or automated translation wrapper.

title: No-AI Language Path
user: A privacy- or quality-conscious language learner who wants a structured interactive routine without generative AI or opaque personalization.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker specifically seeks an interactive language app/site that does not use LLMs or generative AI because familiar products now do.
A user reports that changing a deck preset silently overwrites desired retention, illustrating the need for visible, trustworthy study settings rather than hidden personalization.

recurrence: A direct 2026 request and a separate 2025 configuration failure both point to demand for learner agency and inspectable rules.
current_workaround: Use scattered Anki decks, textbooks, and podcasts, or accept an app whose AI behavior and personalization are not controllable.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo, Babbel, Busuu, and many newer apps add AI features; Anki is flexible but starts as a blank system. The gap is a transparent routine builder that never sends text to a model.
smallest_useful_product: An offline routine composer combining user-selected listening, reading, speaking, and recall blocks with timer/checklists and plain rule-based progression. Non-goals: chat tutoring, auto-generated exercises, or content licensing.
success_measure: In a four-week beta, 60% of users complete a self-authored routine at least three days/week and can correctly explain every progression rule shown in their plan.
monetization: one-time — its promise is durable local control rather than a metered AI service.
constraints: Prominently commit to no model calls and no telemetry by default; user-provided links/files must remain private; avoid claims that a fixed routine produces fluency.
why_distinct: The product’s value is inspectable non-generative structure, not an LLM tutor with a privacy toggle.

title: Walk & Talk Rehearsal
user: A language learner walking or commuting who needs on-demand speaking prompts and deliberate replay without needing a live tutor, partner, or cloud recording.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner asks for an on-demand Italian coach that can be spoken with while walking, particularly for pronunciation practice.
A feature request for smart preset assignment shows active users want study settings to adapt to their actual review profile rather than require blanket configuration.

recurrence: The 2025 walking request is concrete; a separate active-learning community also requests less manual adaptation, making hands-free contextual rehearsal a practical niche.
current_workaround: Book a tutor, talk to an AI chatbot, shadow a podcast without prompts, or record voice memos and never review them.
incumbents_and_gap: Pimsleur provides scripted audio and conversational AI apps provide open chat; neither gives a local, user-authored scenario deck with timed silent rehearsal and optional recording review.
smallest_useful_product: A mobile-first PWA that plays user-authored scenario prompts, gives a configurable silent speaking gap, lets users optionally record locally, and schedules a later replay. Non-goals: speech grading, native-speaker matching, or generated dialogue.
success_measure: At least 50% of pilot users complete 12 walking sessions in 30 days and replay at least one saved response in a later session.
monetization: one-time — recording stays on the device and no recurrent inference cost exists.
constraints: Microphone permission is optional and recordings never upload; clearly warn users about outdoor awareness; provide text-only mode and accessible controls.
why_distinct: It rehearses user-owned situations in a safe audio cadence rather than pretending to be a fluent conversational agent.

title: Skill Drill Studio
user: A teacher, bootcamp instructor, or self-learner who needs to turn a small procedural skill into short browser drills with immediate deterministic feedback.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner built a Vim trainer because reading tutorials did not retain commands; the desired loop is short interactive drills with immediate feedback and repetition.
A user requests a one-click application of recommended learning/relearning steps, underscoring demand for practical guidance that reduces configuration burden.

recurrence: A 2025 maker and a 2026 scheduler user both seek a tighter practice loop with less setup; procedural learning is poorly served by text cards alone.
current_workaround: Make a custom web page, assign a worksheet, use flashcards for actions, or repeatedly re-read tutorials.
incumbents_and_gap: TypingClub and specialized trainers handle preset skills; H5P offers broad authoring. The gap is a tiny no-account creator for command/order/matching drills that works from a teacher’s own examples.
smallest_useful_product: A static web authoring tool for three drill types—ordered steps, exact command input, and image hotspot—with deterministic answer checks and shareable JSON files. Non-goals: arbitrary code execution, AI question generation, LMS replacement, or student profiles.
success_measure: Ten pilot authors publish a drill in under 15 minutes, and 70% of learner attempts show improvement between first and third run.
monetization: free — portable drill files and classroom sharing depend on zero-friction access.
constraints: Never execute learner-entered commands; sanitize all authored HTML/media; accessibility requires keyboard paths and non-color-only feedback.
why_distinct: It is constrained active-practice authoring for procedural skills, not a generic quiz builder or an AI worksheet generator.

title: Classroom Algorithm Cards
user: An elementary teacher or volunteer teaching a one-off computing lesson who needs printable, collaborative, unplugged activities that make sequencing and debugging visible.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent returning to teach 4th/5th graders asks for help improving an introductory software-development classroom activity after a successful PB&J sequencing demo.
Anki contributors request flexible grading and configurable answer keys, reflecting a broader need to recognize multiple valid ways learners can express a solution.

recurrence: A concrete 2025 elementary-classroom request and a separate flexible-answer request point to the same teaching need: make process observable without falsely marking alternative reasoning wrong.
current_workaround: Improvise a PB&J demo, download random worksheets, or use a screen-based coding game that may not fit a single classroom period.
incumbents_and_gap: Code.org and Scratch provide strong curricula, but a visiting adult often needs a 30-minute, device-free, printable sequence/debug kit with teacher cues.
smallest_useful_product: A static generator for printable role cards, instruction cards, challenge cards, and a one-page facilitation guide for 20–40 minute sequencing/debugging games. Non-goals: a full computer-science curriculum, student accounts, or AI-generated lesson plans.
success_measure: At least 15 educators run a complete activity from download to wrap-up in one period, and 80% say setup took under ten minutes.
monetization: free — individual teachers and volunteers need immediate classroom access; optional themed packs can follow only if requested.
constraints: Use original, permissively licensed illustrations; meet print accessibility needs; avoid collecting child data; include teacher safety and group-management notes.
why_distinct: It serves the overlooked one-off, unplugged lesson with multiple-valid-answer facilitation rather than competing with a year-long coding platform.

title: Comprehensible Input Log
user: A language self-learner using books, podcasts, and videos who needs to choose material near their level and see whether input is becoming understandable without a gamified course.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner asking how to learn spoken German receives the recommendation to use comprehensible input—material understood at roughly 90%—alongside practical conversation goals.
A request to resume optimization from prior state shows that personal learning history is valuable and should not require restarting expensive analysis each time.

recurrence: The 2025 language question names level-appropriate input as a key choice, while a 2026 learning-system issue reinforces the value of persistent personal history over reset-based tools.
current_workaround: Guess from content labels, keep notes in a spreadsheet, rely on a platform’s opaque level, or consume material that is much too difficult.
incumbents_and_gap: LingQ tracks imported reading and graded-reader catalogs label levels; neither provides a lightweight, source-agnostic local log of understood vs. looked-up segments across any media.
smallest_useful_product: An offline log where users save a source, duration/pages, self-rate understanding, record up to three recurring unknown words, and get a trend view plus a simple next-source target. Non-goals: automatic transcription, language-level certification, and content hosting.
success_measure: After four weeks, 60% of pilot users log eight sources and show a stable or improving self-rated comprehension trend while reducing abandonment of sources midway.
monetization: free — a private cross-source log needs no server and benefits from easy export.
constraints: Self-ratings are subjective and must not be presented as proficiency scores; no copyrighted media is uploaded; local export/import is required.
why_distinct: It helps learners calibrate their own real-world input selection, not serve another closed library or pretend to assess fluency.
